newsitem.title: UK: Commonwealth split over imposing Nigeria sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth split over imposing Nigeria sanctions.

text.p: Commonwealth ministers gather in New York this weekend to decide whether to impose sanctions on Nigeria but officials say deepening splits among member states could torpedo the meeting.
"This is turning out to be a real mess," said one senior Commonwealth diplomat who asked not to be named.
The eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) agreed a set of sanctions against Nigeria in May to propel the military government toward democracy.
But in June CMAG said the measures -- including a ban on sporting links and arms sales -- would be frozen until the New York meeting to give Nigeria a chance for further talks.

The Commonwealth, a grouping of Britain and its former colonies and protectorates, suspended oil-rich Nigeria last November after the execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority-rights activists.
CMAG members such as Canada are losing patience with the government of General Sani Abacha and say that only a hard line approach will bear results, but others take a softer approach.

Relations among CMAG states were further eroded when the group called off a planned fact-finding mission to Nigeria last month after Abuja refused to let ministers meet human rights campaigners and opposition groups.
Nigeria says it wants to discuss its suspension from the Commonwealth before expanding the dialogue to other topics.

Some CMAG members such as Zimbabwe want the fact-finding mission to go ahead to keep the lines of communication open with Abuja but Canada and New Zealand say this would be pointless without guarantees of access to opposition members.
"None of us can see any great good news coming out of the New York meeting, whatever angle you look at it from," said a British official.
Abacha last year set out a plan to restore civilian rule by October 1998, which CMAG says is too long.
Some Commonwealth officials expressed irritation with Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, saying he was needlessly antagonising the Nigerians.

"Axworthy seems to have lost the script on this one. He does not understand that the Nigerians are a very proud people and you have to try to flatter them by making them feel important," said one official who asked not to be identified.
Axworthy, irritated by what he saw as Commonwealth inertia on Nigeria, announced after the June CMAG meeting that Canada would unilaterally apply the agreed sanctions.

But most Commonwealth officials agree the measures are little more than an irritant and say only an embargo on oil sales -- which most observers said would be virtually impossible to impose -- could damage the Nigerian government.

Diplomats said Washington was backing away from the idea of imposing its own sanctions on the grounds that such measures should be coordinated with the European Union, but this approach has not found favour everywhere.

"To be effective, the American approach should be backed by specific sanction threats," the New York Times said last week, calling for a ban on all U.S. investment. The United States buys 40 percent of its oil from Nigeria.
"Effective American diplomacy with Nigeria requires the threat and use of sanctions. General Abacha has proved to be the kind of man who listens to nothing else."
CMAG comprises Malaysia, Zimbabwe, Jamaica, Ghana, Britain, New Zealand, South Africa and Canada.
